task.goal: Design a fair test to determine whether a new biodegradable packing insert protects fragile ceramic mugs as well as the current insert.
hard_constraints: A workshop has 60 mugs, a basic drop rig, and 30 inserts of each type; no shipment of intentionally damaged goods.
Account for variation in mug batches and drop orientation; define damage criteria before testing.
Include a stopping rule for excessive breakage and do not claim equivalence from a nonsignificant result.
task.available_resources: Two staff and a camera for recording test outcomes.
task.expected_result: A feasible comparative test and decision rule.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Batch-matched, randomized drop test with an explicit equivalence decision
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use all 60 mugs in 30 matched pairs, with one mug per insert type. Match each pair by manufacturing batch and, where possible, mug model and visible condition. Randomly assign inserts within pairs. This controls batch variation; randomization prevents staff from allocating stronger-looking mugs to a preferred insert.

Before testing, specify one drop height representative of actual handling and three relevant orientations, such as base, side, and handle-side impact. Allocate ten pairs to each orientation, balancing batches across orientations as closely as possible. Each mug receives one drop in identical outer packaging, with its assigned orientation shared by its partner. Randomize pair order and which member drops first. The comparison therefore covers this defined, equally weighted orientation mix, not every shipping condition.

Define failure beforehand: any new crack, chip, detached handle, or breakage. Photograph each mug before and after testing under consistent lighting. Record cosmetic scuffs separately. Have one staff member operate the rig and the other inspect mugs using coded photographs that conceal insert identity where feasible. Resolve uncertain damage classifications using a written rule before revealing assignments.

Agree on the largest acceptable difference in failure rates before testing—for example, an illustrative margin of ±10 percentage points, subject to business justification. Equivalence requires the entire prespecified 90% confidence interval for the new-minus-current failure-rate difference to lie inside that margin. Use a paired-binomial interval method suitable for sparse outcomes. A nonsignificant difference does not establish equivalence. With only 30 mugs per type, an inconclusive result is likely, even if observed outcomes look similar.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First inspect rig alignment, release height, packaging consistency, and orientation placement without dropping mugs. Then conduct the randomized comparison, retaining photographs and pair-level outcomes. The current insert is the direct comparator; excess failures with the new insert would challenge its protective claim.

Check the stopping rule after every completed pair: stop the entire test if either insert reaches five failures. This illustrative excessive-breakage threshold must be accepted before starting. An early stop permits no equivalence claim; report the outcomes and safety concern. If all pairs finish, calculate the prespecified interval and report equivalence only if its bounds qualify; otherwise report inconclusive evidence or a demonstrated difference, as applicable.

The plan needs the stated rig, camera, two staff, standardized outer packaging, and access to a suitable statistical calculation. Quarantine every tested mug and ship none of them. Results remain uncertain for untested heights, vibration, moisture, and repeated impacts.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Compare protective endurance under a repeated-drop sequence
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Measure how long each package protects its mug through a predefined handling sequence. This tests cumulative protection, including insert deformation after earlier impacts, rather than protection against one isolated drop.

Form 30 pairs matched by manufacturing batch and mug model. Randomly assign one current and one biodegradable insert within each pair. Use identical outer packaging. Each mug receives up to four drops at a justified handling height, stopping its sequence at first damage. Prespecify four orientation sequences that balance base, side, and handle-side impacts across drop positions; assign the same sequence to both members of each pair and balance sequences across batches. Alternate or randomize which member drops first.

Before testing, define damage as any new chip, crack, detached handle, or fracture, with photographs of each mug before testing and after each drop. The outcome is the number of damage-free drops completed, from zero to four. A mug surviving all four scores four; do not infer its ultimate failure threshold.

Prespecify a business-justified noninferiority margin in mean damage-free drops. Adoption requires the lower one-sided 95% confidence bound for the paired new-minus-current mean difference to exceed the negative margin. Use a statistical method valid for paired, bounded discrete outcomes, such as conservative exact multinomial confidence bounds. A nonsignificant difference is insufficient. Also require the current insert to meet a predefined absolute performance floor so that two poorly protecting inserts cannot qualify together.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
First inspect release height, orientation reproducibility, and package fit without dropping mugs. Then run one matched pair through its assigned sequence and continue only if recording and orientation control work; retain this pair in the analysis if the protocol remains unchanged. The current insert provides the direct falsifying comparator: substantially earlier damage with the biodegradable insert contradicts comparable endurance.

Stop the entire experiment immediately when either type accumulates five damaged mugs, including during a pair. An early stop permits no noninferiority claim. Otherwise complete all 30 pairs and apply the prespecified confidence-bound decision; failure to qualify means insufficient evidence or inferior endurance, depending on the interval.

Two staff can operate and inspect, using coded photographs for independent outcome review where feasible. The plan requires standardized boxes, a recording sheet, and statistical calculation support. Quarantine every tested mug; ship none. At most 240 drops are needed. Thirty pairs may yield an inconclusive result. Conclusions apply to this repeated-impact sequence; transport relevance depends on whether its height, orientations, and cumulative impacts represent actual handling.

EXPAND.title: Estimate protection across a range of impact energies
EXPAND.proposal:
Compare the inserts’ fragility curves: the probability of mug damage as drop height increases. This tests whether the biodegradable insert provides comparable protection across a defined handling range, including whether its protection deteriorates more sharply at higher impacts. Each mug receives just one drop, avoiding cumulative damage.

Before testing, choose three heights spanning a plausible handling range, based on existing workshop knowledge. If realistic handling heights are unknown, label this a laboratory comparison rather than shipping qualification. Form 30 pairs matched by mug batch, model, and initial condition; randomly allocate one insert of each type within each pair. Assign ten pairs to each height. Balance base, side, and handle-side orientations across heights and batches as closely as possible, with both members of each pair receiving the same orientation and height. Randomize pair order and drop order within pairs. Use identical outer packaging and packing procedures.

Prespecify damage as any new chip, crack, handle separation, or fracture. Photograph mugs before and after each drop; one staff member operates the rig while the other assesses coded images with insert identity concealed where feasible. Record scuffs separately. Retain all tested mugs for inspection; ship none as part of this experiment.

Before seeing outcomes, specify a justified maximum acceptable excess damage probability and an absolute protection requirement. Fit a prespecified, simple height–damage model accounting for pairing and orientation. Adoption requires a simultaneous one-sided 95% upper confidence band for new-minus-current damage probability to remain below the margin throughout the tested range, plus satisfaction of the absolute requirement. This establishes noninferiority only within that range. Sparse failures, model dependence, and ten pairs per height may leave the result inconclusive; nonsignificance cannot establish equivalence.
EXPAND.experiment: The smallest diagnostic check is whether the current insert shows a useful transition from mostly intact to some damaged mugs across the selected heights. Inspect its raw outcomes alongside the fitted curve; a flat or badly fitting response undermines the proposed mechanism and prevents model-based adoption. Check results against direct paired comparisons at each height so that smoothing cannot hide a local disadvantage. Use a prespecified sparse-data analysis method; if it cannot produce reliable confidence bounds, report inconclusive. Review after every completed pair and stop the entire experiment once six mugs have failed, finishing neither additional pairs nor higher-height trials. Count all observed damage and treat an early stop as inconclusive for adoption. Implementation needs only the 60 mugs, 60 inserts, existing rig, two staff, camera, and statistical software with someone able to construct simultaneous confidence bounds.

REFINE.title: Candidate 0 repair: make damage assessment a blinded physical inspection
REFINE.proposal: Select original candidate 0: its single-drop, batch-matched randomized comparison is the most feasible direct test with 60 mugs. Its specific weakness is relying on coded photographs to classify damage: photographs can miss fine cracks or chips inside the mug or around handle joints, potentially making both inserts appear equally protective. Replace photo-based classification with a standardized, blinded physical inspection before and after dropping. The rig operator removes packaging out of the inspector’s view and presents each mug under a neutral code. The second staff member checks the interior, exterior, rim, base, handle and both handle joints under consistent lighting; photographs document findings. Prespecify that any new visible crack, chip, detached handle or fracture is failure, and unresolved suspected damage counts as failure. Prerequisites are a concealed assignment key, a surface checklist and baseline condition records. Retain candidate 0’s pairing, randomized orientation allocation, confidence-interval decision, excessive-breakage stopping rule and quarantine of all tested mugs. The remaining limit is that visual inspection cannot exclude hidden microcracks or establish protection under untested shipping conditions.
REFINE.experiment: Before dropping anything, rehearse coded presentation and the complete inspection checklist on two allocated mugs, confirming that the inspector cannot see packaging or assignments. For the first scheduled pair, record a photograph-only judgment before the blinded physical inspection. A crack or chip found only in person falsifies the adequacy of photograph-only assessment. Physical inspection remains the prespecified outcome method for every mug regardless of this check; retain the first pair in the comparison. If coding reveals insert identity or any surface cannot be inspected consistently, correct the workflow before further drops. This adds no mugs or drops and uses the existing two staff and camera.
